title: US dollar shipments to Iraq are a molehill, not a mountain
gist: The roughly $1-1.5 billion of US physical dollar shipments withheld from Iraq during the Iran war had no measurable economic effect — the dinar parallel rate was flat March to July, oil revenues kept flowing into the FRBNY account, and the CBI still sold $18.3 billion of reserves for imports. Cash dollars have fallen from 7.9 percent of CBI reserves in 2014 to 1.5 percent in 2025 as Iraq's post-November-2022 formal banking transition pushed 95 percent of international transfers through correspondent-banked top-tier banks.

insights.claim: The United States halted dollar cash shipments to Iraq for about three months as the Iran war ramped up before resuming them in early July, and media coverage of both the halt and the resumption reflected persistent misconceptions about Iraq's dollar accounts at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
entities: Federal Reserve Bank of New York
insights.so_what: Headlines conflating cash shipments with Iraq's access to oil revenue are a recurring mispricing source for Iraq-linked assets and dinar expectations.
insights.locator: As the Iran war ramped up

insights.claim: Two specific misconceptions circulate about the halt: that it deprived the Iraqi government of its own oil revenues held at the FRBNY leaving it unable to pay public sector salaries and pensions, and that the shipments are needed to keep Iraq's dollar-dependent economy running or to maintain the dinar peg.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Both claims are testable and false on the data — a checklist for filtering noise from genuine Iraq financial stress signals.
insights.locator: One misconception is that the halt deprived

insights.claim: The misconceptions have roots in the economic and financial chaos that followed the 2003 US invasion of Iraq but have persisted even as Iraq has moved toward a formal banking system and away from cash-based informality, a shift that accelerated since late 2022.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Analytical frameworks built on post-2003 Iraq are now structurally stale; risk models need updating to the post-2022 banking regime.

themes.theme: How the two FRBNY accounts actually work

insights.claim: Iraq holds two distinct and structurally different dollar accounts at the FRBNY — one where oil export revenues are deposited by buyers, and a separate Central Bank of Iraq foreign reserves account from which cash dollars are withdrawn and flown to Iraq — linked only through the conversion of dollar oil revenues into dinars.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Because the accounts are separate, a cash shipment freeze does not touch oil revenue receipt — the mechanism that makes the alarmist read wrong.

insights.claim: The share of the Central Bank of Iraq's reserves held as cash dollars fell from 7.9 percent of total reserves at the end of 2014 to 1.5 percent at the end of 2025.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: A five-fold decline in cash intensity means the physical dollar channel is a rounding error in Iraq's external finance — the leverage Washington once had has shrunk.
insights.locator: However, the share of the CBI’s reserves held as cash dollars

insights.claim: Media reports indicated at least two shipments were withheld, including one worth $500 million, between the first US-Israeli strikes against Iran in late February and the July resumption, implying a total withheld of roughly $1 billion to $1.5 billion.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Sizes the disruption at $1-1.5bn, which is trivial against the $18.3bn of reserve sales over the same window.
insights.locator: Media reports indicated that at least two shipments were withheld

themes.theme: The fiscal and FX flow data

insights.claim: Iraq earned $10.9 billion of oil revenues from March through May deposited into its FRBNY oil revenue account, of which the Ministry of Finance sold $8.1 billion to the Central Bank of Iraq for dinars to help fund $22.2 billion of budget expenditures, with the remainder funded by $5 billion of non-oil revenues and domestic borrowing.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Reveals an Iraqi fiscal gap — $22.2bn of spending against $10.9bn oil plus $5bn non-oil over three months — filled by domestic borrowing, the real vulnerability to watch.
insights.locator: Iraq earned oil revenues of $10.9 billion from March through May

insights.claim: Between March and June the Central Bank of Iraq sold $18.3 billion from its foreign reserves to Iraqi businesses and individuals via banks to pay for imports and other cross-border transactions, drawn from the same FRBNY reserves account that funds the cash shipments.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: $18.3bn of electronic reserve sales versus ~$1.5bn of withheld cash shows where Iraq's actual dollar access lives — the wire channel, not the cargo plane.
insights.locator: Between March and June, the CBI sold $18.3 billion

insights.claim: The value of the dollar against the Iraqi dinar in the parallel market remained flat between March and July, indicating the halt in cash dollar shipments produced no panic demand for dollars among Iraqis.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: The parallel-market rate is the cleanest real-time stress gauge for Iraq dollar policy — flat means no transmission, and it is publicly observable.
insights.locator: At the same time, the value of the dollar against the Iraqi dinar

insights.claim: The only visible effect of a sustained halt would have been a squeeze on cash dollars available at airports for Iraqis traveling abroad, who could still have used bank cards, and the CBI continued supplying travelers — particularly for the Hajj — with $600 million of physical dollars from its vaults between March and June.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Quantifies the entire affected use case at $600m of travel cash, confirming the policy lever is largely symbolic.
insights.locator: The only visible effect, had the shipments remained halted

insights.claim: When the United States last suspended dollar transfers to Iraq in 2015 amid concerns dollars were being used by the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham and Iranian banks, the dollar's value against the dinar in the parallel market rose about 11 percent, reflecting a sharp increase in dollar demand.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: The 2015 baseline (11 percent dinar move) versus 2026 (zero) is the clearest possible measure of how much US cash-channel leverage over Iraq has decayed.
insights.locator: In 2015, the United States stopped the transfers

insights.claim: The withholding of dollar cash shipments did not affect the Iraqi government's ability to receive oil revenues in dollars at the FRBNY, convert them into dinars, or fund domestic expenditures, nor did it constrain the CBI's ability to use foreign reserves to finance imports.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Cash-shipment suspension is not an effective sanctions instrument against Iraq anymore; genuine pressure would require touching the FRBNY oil account or correspondent access.

themes.theme: Iraq's formalization of cross-border payments since 2022

insights.claim: The Central Bank of Iraq updated its regulations for providing dollars for foreign transfers in November 2022, bringing Iraq's cross-border fund transfers in line with global standards, in a system that resulted from two years of planning by the FRBNY, the US Treasury, the CBI, and the Ministry of Finance.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: US institutions co-designed Iraq's payment architecture, meaning influence now runs through correspondent-banking compliance rather than physical cash.

insights.claim: International transfers have shifted to Iraq's strongest banks — those with correspondent relationships with major international banks and whose transactions are reviewed by an international risk-management agency nominated by the FRBNY — rising from 40 percent of transactions in 2023 when the channel started to 95 percent in January-May 2026.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: A 40-to-95 percent consolidation in three years concentrates Iraq's external payments in a handful of compliant banks — a winner-take-most shift in Iraqi banking.
insights.locator: First, international transfers have increasingly shifted

insights.claim: The post-November-2022 cash distribution system is among the most closely monitored in the world, capturing passport numbers, travel destinations, travel frequency, and amounts obtained for Iraqis receiving cash dollars, giving authorities the information to investigate travelers and related parties.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Undermines the premise that Iraqi cash dollars are an untraceable leakage channel to sanctioned actors — the stated rationale for halts is weaker than assumed.
insights.locator: But the table does not capture another important change

insights.claim: The November 2022 changes represented a seismic shift for a cash-dominated economy in which large informal sectors drove the bulk of economic activity, and the initial shock combined with subsequent CBI and government measures fast-tracked the transition toward banking and formal economic activity.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Forced formalization creates a multi-year growth runway for Iraqi banks, payments, and credit intermediation — a structural investment theme in a frontier market.
insights.locator: At the time, those changes represented a seismic shift

insights.claim: Iraq's economy and particularly its financial sector have changed dramatically since 2003, and the risks that come with that evolution cannot be properly understood or addressed through outdated assumptions.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Analysts using post-invasion mental models will systematically misread Iraqi policy shocks — an exploitable information asymmetry in frontier markets coverage.
insights.quote: It’s about time media coverage caught up.
